name: Daria Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a stock hand at Harrow Farms, which runs about four hundred outdoor sows, the breeding pigs, plus three hundred hectares of wheat and barley that mostly goes into their feed. My day starts at seven with the farrowing paddocks, the little huts where sows have their piglets, checking every hut for new litters and any piglets that got squashed. Then feeding, water troughs, moving electric fences, and in spring and autumn I get pulled onto the tractor for the arable side.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the piglets, obviously, everyone does, but I really like the problem-solving. A trough's leaking, a sow won't feed her litter, the fence keeps shorting, you work it out. What wears me out is the mud from November to March, and Steve the manager, who's lovely but wants everything written on paper, in pen, like it's 1985.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I ask it about pig health before I bother the vet, I use it to plan my fencing runs, and I've been using it to draw up a business plan for a little pork-box idea of my own. I'm two years in and still learning the basics, but I'm the one who sets up the new apps for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful and people should try it, especially farmers, because it saves hours. I'd probably post something about how I use it for pig health questions. Some of the older ones would roll their eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my pork-box idea gets easier to run. The website, the adverts, the orders, I can do most of it at night with AI. It doesn't change Harrow at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rent the bit of rough grazing my uncle has, about two hectares, and start with twelve weaners, young pigs, in the spring. That's maybe two thousand from savings, which is about half of what Tom and I have. Keep the Harrow job, obviously, it's the safe money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and keen. I like having a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Half your savings is a lot. Does Tom agree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He agrees with conditions, which is Tom. He said fine, but if it loses money by Christmas, the pigs go to market and we don't do it again. That's fair, I'd say the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Tom do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He drives a milk tanker, collecting from dairy farms across the county at four in the morning. We see each other at tea time and that's about it. He thinks AI is a fad but he uses the sat nav more than anyone I know.

S0.say: I'd say it's useful and farmers should try it because it saves hours. I'd post about using it for pig health questions, even if the older ones roll their eyes.
S0.think: I think it makes my pork-box idea easier, since I can run the website, adverts and orders at night with AI. It doesn't change Harrow at all.
S0.do: Rents two hectares of her uncle's rough grazing and starts twelve weaners in spring, spending about two thousand, roughly half the couple's savings. Keeps her Harrow job as the safe income.
S0.feel: Calm and keen, because she likes having a plan.
S0.quote: He agrees with conditions, which is Tom. He said fine, but if it loses money by Christmas, the pigs go to market and we don't do it again.
S0.fieldNote: Daria thinks like a business owner even as a junior, and she uses AI as a partner for her side plan. She'd risk half the savings but with a clear stop rule. Her partner Tom acts as the brake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow is good, it gives people like me time to get ahead of it. But fewer beginners is a problem, farms already can't find staff. I'd say we need more apprenticeships, ones that actually pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd see a gap. If tasks disappear slowly, Harrow will want someone who understands the new kit, the cameras and sensors, and I'm already the app person. It could be my way up faster than waiting ten years behind Steve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Harrow to send me on any course about pig monitoring, the cameras that spot sick or lame pigs. I'd volunteer to run a trial. And I'd keep the pork boxes going on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe a little uneasy for the people who don't get a start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there someone you know who didn't get a start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Liam applied to three farms last spring and none of them took him, because none of them could afford to train someone. He's stacking shelves now. He's good with animals, too, better than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said waiting ten years behind Steve. Is that how it feels now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. Steve's forty-eight and he's not going anywhere, and there's only one manager job. I'm not complaining, he's fair, but if I want to move up I have to make a new job rather than wait for his.

S1.say: I'd say slow change gives people time to get ahead of it, but fewer beginners is a problem when farms already can't find staff. We need apprenticeships that actually pay.
S1.think: I see a gap: Harrow will want someone who understands the cameras and sensors, and I'm already the app person. It could get me up faster than waiting ten years behind Steve.
S1.do: Asks Harrow to send her on pig monitoring courses and volunteers to run a camera trial. Keeps the pork-box side business running.
S1.feel: Calm, a little uneasy for people who don't get a start.
S1.quote: If I want to move up I have to make a new job rather than wait for his.
S1.fieldNote: She reads slow change as an opening for herself and says so. Her cousin's story shows the cost for others, and she noticed it without being asked twice. Her centre view comes out as practical: paid apprenticeships, not blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's tough on office workers and politicians should stop arguing and do something useful, like help with retraining. I'd also say, gently, that farms are hiring, come and look. That would probably annoy people online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me it's mostly fine. My pork-box customers are office people, though, the ones who pay extra for outdoor-reared. If they get pay cuts, they buy cheaper pork, and my side plan gets harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd change the pork boxes to smaller, cheaper ones, half boxes and sausages, not the fancy cuts. I'd use AI to look at what sells and drop the rest. I'd hold back from buying more weaners until I see the orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a busy way. I'd be fiddling with prices every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's in a half box, and what does it cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sausages, mince, a few chops and a bit of belly, about eight kilos. I'd want to sell it for around sixty and still make a little. The AI helped me work out the price, but I checked it against the butcher on Market Street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would any of the new AI jobs interest you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one about farm data, if it was part time and near home. I don't want to leave pigs for a laptop full time. The point of AI for me is that it lets me stay outside more, not less.

S2.say: I'd say it's tough on office workers and politicians should stop arguing and help with retraining. I'd also say farms are hiring, which might annoy people online.
S2.think: It's mostly fine for me, but my pork-box customers are office workers who pay extra for outdoor-reared meat. If their pay is cut, they buy cheaper pork and my side plan suffers.
S2.do: Switches to cheaper half boxes of about eight kilos at around sixty, using AI to check what sells. Delays buying more weaners until orders are clear.
S2.feel: Uneasy, but busy with it, adjusting prices every night.
S2.quote: The point of AI for me is that it lets me stay outside more, not less.
S2.fieldNote: She spots that office layoffs reach her through her customers. Her response is quick and practical, changing the product rather than worrying. She double-checks AI against a real butcher, which is a nice detail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains should be shared fairly, some tax on the share boom, help for people out of work. But I wouldn't join the shouting, I'd rather just get on. People will want food whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this picture is all right for me. Physical jobs are safe, and people with booming shares want posh pork, so my top boxes might sell again. The worry is house prices, because Tom and I wanted to buy in about five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the pork boxes harder, aimed at the people doing well. I'd maybe take on a second paddock. And I'd talk to Tom about whether buying is still realistic, or if we rent long term and put the money into the pigs instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Good for business, bad for the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had to choose between the house and the pigs, which wins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, right now, the pigs, and that's why Tom and I argue. He wants a front door that's ours. I want a business that's ours. We both think the other is being a bit unrealistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you feel bad selling to the people doing well while others lose jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, yes. But if I don't sell to them, someone else will, and I need the money to keep Harrow's wage as backup. I'd keep a cheap box for local people too, that matters to me.

S3.say: I'd say gains should be shared, with some tax on the share boom and help for the jobless. But I wouldn't join the shouting, because people will want food whatever happens.
S3.think: This picture is all right for me: physical jobs are safe and people with booming shares want posh pork. My worry is house prices, since Tom and I hoped to buy in five years.
S3.do: Markets pork boxes to better-off buyers and considers a second paddock. Talks with Tom about renting long term and putting money into the pigs instead of a house, while keeping a cheap local box.
S3.feel: Uneasy: good for business, bad for the house.
S3.quote: He wants a front door that's ours. I want a business that's ours.
S3.fieldNote: The tension in this household is house versus business, and she was honest that she'd pick the pigs. She feels a bit uneasy selling to the winners but keeps a cheap box for locals. Business sums, not fear, drive her answers here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the last picture. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots on farms can be good, if workers get trained to run them and the money from it is shared fairly. I'd say don't fight it, shape it. Some people at Harrow wouldn't want to hear that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my Harrow job is at risk, because feeding, fencing and checking huts is exactly what a robot with a camera could do. And Tom's in trouble too, because self-driving lorries would come for tankers. That's both our incomes at once, which is what scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Harrow to make me the robot person, the one who sets them up and fixes the faults, and do the training whatever it cost. I'd grow the pork boxes so we'd have a second income. And I'd sit with Tom and plan for his job ending, maybe he works the pigs with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because I'd have things to do, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, okay, we've got four months saved and twelve pigs, so let's make it twenty-four. He'd laugh, then he'd go quiet. Then he'd ask what a pig trailer costs, and I'd know he was in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is your own pig business safe from robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, but a small business sells the story, outdoor pigs and a real person. People pay for my face on the label. A robot could do the feeding, and honestly I'd let it, if I could afford one.

S4.say: I'd say robots on farms can be good if workers are trained and the money is shared fairly. Don't fight it, shape it, even if some at Harrow wouldn't like hearing it.
S4.think: My Harrow job is at risk, because a robot with a camera could feed, fence and check huts. Tom's tanker job is at risk too, so both our incomes go at once.
S4.do: Asks Harrow to make her the robot person and pays for the training if needed. Grows the pork boxes from twelve to around twenty-four pigs and plans with Tom for him to work the pigs if his tanker job ends.
S4.feel: Anxious but not panicked, because she has things to do.
S4.quote: Then he'd ask what a pig trailer costs, and I'd know he was in.
S4.fieldNote: The threat to both incomes at once is what worries her, not robots as such. Her answer is to grow the side business and become the robot person. She'd happily let a robot feed her own pigs, which was a surprising and honest moment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's all five. Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one, because it hits me and Tom together. What would help is cheap loans for small farm businesses, so people like us can start something instead of waiting to be laid off. And training on the robots that's free for farm workers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask what we'd build, not just what we'd lose. Everyone asks what you're scared of. I've got twelve pigs and a plan, and nobody ever asks about that.

headlineQuote: He wants a front door that's ours. I want a business that's ours.
portrait: Daria is a 27-year-old stock hand on an outdoor pig and arable farm, two years in, who uses AI daily and is planning a small pork-box business with twelve weaners on her uncle's land. She's pragmatic and middle-of-the-road, prefers shaping change to fighting it, and doesn't blame anyone. Through the pictures she keeps adjusting her side business to who has money, and her real tension at home is house versus business with her partner Tom. The robot picture makes her anxious because her job and Tom's tanker driving would both be at risk, but her answer is to grow the pigs and become the farm's robot person.
biggestWorry: The fast AI and robots picture, because robots could take her farm job and self-driving lorries could take Tom's at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans for small farm businesses so workers can start something of their own, and free robot training for farm workers.
